page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard3.Flex.32-512 is an x86_64 virtual machine instance powered by an Intel Xeon 8358 processor operating at a base frequency of 2.6 GHz. It is provisioned with 32 dedicated physical cores and 64 virtual central processing units (vCPUs) with two hardware threads per core. The instance provides 512.0 GB of system memory, creating an allocation ratio of 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU.

This hardware configuration features no GPU acceleration and does not bundle local storage, requiring network-attached storage solutions to support persistent disk access. A single complimentary public IPv4 address is provided. The allocation of 8.0 GB per core yields high memory density on dedicated enterprise Intel hardware, though deployments must balance compute performance against the input/output characteristics of remote storage.

VM.Standard3.Flex.32-512 is structured for workloads that require large active memory footprints without requiring discrete hardware accelerators. Suitable applications include in-memory databases, distributed caching nodes, memory-intensive data transformation pipelines, ETL batch processing, and high-concurrency enterprise web services.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard3.Flex.32-512 is an enterprise virtual machine instance built on the x86_64 architecture using an Intel Xeon 8358 processor clocked at 2.6 GHz. The server features 32 dedicated physical cores, 64 vCPUs via multithreading, and 512.0 GB of system RAM, maintaining an 8.0 GB memory-to-vCPU ratio. It provides one complimentary public IPv4 address, contains no GPU accelerators, and includes no local storage volumes, relying entirely on network-attached storage for disk operations. The substantial memory footprint paired with dedicated compute cores delivers balanced capacity for memory-intensive enterprise tasks without the expense of discrete GPU hardware. VM.Standard3.Flex.32-512 is appropriate for large in-memory databases, memory-centric caching tiers, big data batch processing, ETL workloads, and large-scale web backends.
